11og6x0.title: Gaming storefronts are facing a Slop Grenade problem | Opinion
11og6x0.content:
Players and creators alike dislike AI-created games, but digital storefronts are ill-equipped for the avalanche of slop that threatens to tank discoverability and turn away consumers

Image credit: Valve

There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.
At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.
This is, of course, a microcosm of broader efforts by tech giants to convince the world of the inevitability of AI permeating every facet of life and work. It follows the same playbook and rests on the same foundation of dubiously conflating many different tools and systems, including deep learning models that predate LLMs by many years, under the single banner of "AI usage".
In game development, that can mean all manner of rhetorical sleight of hand. Anything from programmers using Copilot autocompletions, to 2D artists using a background removal tool in Photoshop, to a project manager using the meeting summary tool in Zoom, can all end up counted as a tick in a box and a "studio that's using AI".A good rule of thumb is that when someone pops up every five minutes to dramatically insist something is a fait accompli, that's a pretty sure sign that it's precisely the opposite. Nobody feels the need to convince the world of a new reality when it's actually real.
None of this is to say that plenty of developers and studios aren't experimenting with AI tools or considering how they fit their workflows. Games are a cutting-edge, high-tech industry as well as a creative one. To the extent new AI tools are useful, reliable, and effective, they'll be adopted. People will automate writing tons of boring templates or testing code, and welcome smarter tools for automating parts of the development pipeline for game assets. Nobody in a high-tech industry will turn down genuinely better versions of IDEs or image editors; that doesn't mean they want to fire their art department and replace it with half-assed prompting.
"Nobody in high-tech will turn down better versions of IDEs or image editors; that doesn't mean they want to fire and replace their art department with half-assed prompting"
Even as developers explore useful tools washed ashore amid the storm tide of hype, they're conscious of a massive factor looming over all of this. There's a reason why many dubious, anonymous surveys claim loads of development studios use AI, yet few actual studios proudly say so. Two reasons, really: first, as mentioned, many studios would probably contest that what they're doing constitutes "using AI in development" in the way people actually think of it. The second is that they know that their customers despise the idea of AI in games – a stance that has only become more deeply ingrained among consumers as AI boosters' claims of inevitability have grown more shrill.
Consumers really don't like AI, and the challenge for those hoping to change minds is that the reasons for dislike are varied and largely valid. Some dislike the aesthetic of AI-produced work – many can smell it from a mile off, and it's shocking how many ordinary folks have a viscerally negative reaction to seeing AI artwork or hearing AI-created music. Some hate the ethics of AI, with good reason; the argument for using training data to create a language model looks thin when it creates a model that mimics people's artwork, voice, or image wholesale. Others rail against data centres, economic impacts, or just hate the unlikeable billionaire figureheads of the AI wave itself.Any attempt to normalise extensive AI usage in development will crash hard against that wall. Most consumers want art made by humans and will vote with their wallets to get it. They'll also demand the right to make informed choices, as seen with calls on Steam not only to ensure that AI-created games are clearly labelled, but that consumers have a straightforward way to filter them.
AI boosters like Epic's Tim Sweeney have railed against the labelling of AI-created titles, which is something of an admission in itself; if they were genuinely convinced that AI was poised to be embraced by the world as a valid and welcome creative tool of the future, they wouldn't be so adamant that developers must be allowed to use it under the cover of darkness.
The situation around games developed using AI extensively on the Steam platform bubbled up again a couple of weeks ago when the Steam Next Fest, an event that's meant to showcase hidden gems on the service, turned out to be riddled with lazily churned-out titles filled with AI assets.
Players demanded a strict filter to remove AI titles, a reasonable ask assuming "AI titles" can be defined meaningfully. For the broader industry, this highlights a problem with AI that's rapidly growing out of control, with far larger consequences than any debates over the creative or ethical validity of AI tools. There's an avalanche of slop bearing down on us – and nobody knows how to cope with it yet.
"Tools now churn out game after game filled with IP-infringing assets, letting those willing to pay hefty fees release several titles a week"
To see a miniature example of the chaos coming, look at retro gaming spaces now. In recent months, a niche community devoted to "decomps" – decompiling old, usually abandoned games so they can be re-implemented on modern hardware – has been overtaken by a gigantic wave of AI-driven, automated decompilations of many games, mostly still commercial titles.
These vibe-coded recreations sometimes mash bits of different games in ways that probably have corporate IP lawyers tasting colours and seeing entire new planes of reality. They remain largely a curiosity, yielding more hours of TikTok videos than playtime. However, they have drowned out that corner of the retro gaming space, likely destroying it forever – and in the process, pointed a grim finger at what's coming for other parts of the industry in the near future.The bar to making games was already much lower than in the past, and in general, that lowering has been a good thing. High-quality development tools and the democratisation of distribution platforms have created whole new industry segments and opened doors for exciting, diverse new creative voices; it's not even worth thinking about how creatively barren videogames would have looked over the past decade without that.
What's happening now, however, is that the bar to making something that passes as a game has dropped below ground level. Tools now churn out game after game filled with IP-infringing assets, letting anyone willing to pay a hefty fee release several new titles a week.
This echoes one of the problems encountered by corporations that adopted generative AI in the past couple of years. It's called the "slop grenade" – meaning that people using AI produce massive amounts of reports, emails, and other output materials (no doubt feeling terribly productive in the process), but all of this constitutes a hand grenade of AI slop that explodes on someone else's workload, because eventually someone has to go through everything they've produced.
This is exactly what's happening to gaming storefronts – already on Steam – a massive increase in quickly produced, low-quality games given a vague sheen of professionalism by models trained on countless professionally produced video games.

Slop isn't a new problem, as anyone who's ever dipped a toe past the first page of Nintendo's eShop will recognise | Image credit: Billiam/YouTube

Slop itself isn't a new problem, of course; anyone who watched the early promise of mobile gaming disappear under a torrent of slop knows that, as does anyone who's ever dipped a toe past the first page of Nintendo's online store. Reskins and asset flips are commonplace; many marketplaces teem with games that barely function past the first few screens or that shamelessly aim to rake in some coins from unsuspecting consumers misspelling the names of legitimate titles in their searches.What's new is the sheer scale of what's coming – a scale at which even if every slop title only ekes out a few quid here and there, their cumulative effect could still crash discoverability, destroy marketplaces, and leech massive amounts of revenue away from real, genuine games.
Some creators are sounding the alarm about this; Smash Bros. creator Masahiro Sakurai mentioned in a recent interview that he already sees AI accelerating a flood of unoriginal titles that copy other people's ideas and fill up storefronts with games that can never be profitable. It was interesting to hear this from a Japanese developer in particular, given how positive coverage of AI has generally been in Japan compared to in Western countries.
Solutions can't come from creators; only people who can actually close the gates against the flood of slop, and it's unclear whether they have the will or means to do so.
The system right now will not cope. Platforms like Steam have largely given up on earlier attempts to gatekeep access – people hated when Steam only allowed invited titles, and still hated the greenlight system. So we've ended with what is essentially a free-for-all where any game can launch on Steam if it pays a small fee. That worked, to a degree, for a while. It's about to stop working.
"We need to stop talking about AI as an inevitable future and start talking about how to clear up the inevitable mess it's going to make"
It will stop working because even when Valve stopped holding the gate shut, a gatekeeper remained: making a game, even a bad one, took time, effort, and knowledge. If that gatekeeper is also gone, then we're about to see what a truly open market looks like for the first time in the medium's history. I'm not sure that's what anyone actually wants, least of all real creators who will fight to keep their head above this rising tide of slop.In this, at least, creators and consumers will find themselves allied. The market is making it pretty clear that it doesn't think doing nothing and embracing the slop is an acceptable answer, and platform holders like Steam (and console platform holders, and mobile storefronts) will have to respond to consumer demand eventually, even if they won't respond to creators' pleas.
How to fix the problem is a bigger, thornier issue, and we'll no doubt see some silly fighting-AI-with-AI misfires along the way. The starting point will be a shift in the tone of discussion; we need to stop talking about AI as an inevitable future and start talking about how to clear up the inevitable mess it's going to make.

1r21lf0.title: Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software
1r21lf0.byline: Kate Soule, Luis A Lastras, Subhajit Chaudhury, Abraham Daniels
1r21lf0.content:
Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.
Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass.
Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.
This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.
Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

1uiu4pa.title: Russia drone strike on Ukrainian railway station kills 13
1uiu4pa.content:
Russia drone strike on Ukrainian railway station kills 13

“Civilians preparing for a trip, welcoming or bidding farewell to loved ones faced death and devastation,” said Matthias Schmale, the Humanitarian Coordinator for Ukraine, adding that displaced people and humanitarian workers at a transit centre at the station were left in shock by the nearby explosions.

Media outlets reported that a jet-powered drone hit the station as a train due to travel to Zaporizhzhia stood at a platform. An 11-year-old boy was among the injured, according to regional officials cited in the reports.Rising risks for rail passengersMr. Schmale expressed condolences to the families of those killed on behalf of the UN, noting that train travel is a key means of transportation in Ukraine.Since the start of the year, he said, travellers and railway workers have faced increased risks on every journey due to Russian military strikes and air alerts affecting the safety and reliability of trains.According to figures from Ukraine’s railway operator cited by media outlets, attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.Recent months have seen repeated attacks across the country on civilian infrastructure critical to daily life, including bridges, hospitals, schools, shopping centres and railway stations, Mr. Schmale said.Inured to violence“The images from Dnipro cannot become another story that fades from attention. Behind every casualty is a person, a family and a future changed forever,” he said.“It cannot be repeated often enough that civilians and civilian infrastructure are protected under international humanitarian law.”Aid convoys head for OleshkyMr. Schmale told UN News in an interview on Thursday that preparations to get aid into Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Kherson region, were “accelerating” while a local ceasefire held, and that deliveries could arrive as early as Friday. The ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump and announced by the White House on 23 October, is due to end on the evening of 1 November.Ukraine’s Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has said he is on his way to the town and will accompany residents out.Mr. Schmale said mined roads were a key reason residents had been trapped. He pointed to images of a stretch known locally as the “road of death”.“It’s clear any safe passage both in and out has to have mine clearance preceding it,” he said, adding that reports reaching him confirmed demining was under way.Offer of support ‘not taken up’The UN has no direct role in the evacuation. “We have offered support, but it’s not been taken up,” Mr. Schmale said, adding that none of its partners were involved either.Under established procedure, evacuees will get help once they reach Government-controlled areas. That includes food and other material assistance, and possibly help finding housing. “There’s a high likelihood that we will get involved the minute they are here,” he said.More than 1,000 likely to remainMr. Schmale said estimates varied, but he had heard that 200 to 300 people might leave, “which would leave more than 1,000 there, and they would need support”.He cited accounts from UN human rights monitors, civil society groups and the Ukrainian authorities. The town’s remaining health facility was “barely functional” and short of medicine, he said, and keeping warm through winter amid energy disruption would be a growing challenge. Safe water and public infrastructure were also pressing needs.“Because they’ve been trapped in that place for so long under heavy bombardment, mental health issues should never be overlooked,” he said.

1a37yll.title: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
1a37yll.byline: Avijit Ghosh, Sayeed Choudhury, Greg Tananbaum, Emma Scharfmann, Georgia Channing, Eunice Mercado-Lara, Irene Solaiman
1a37yll.content:
An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.
The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Making publicly funded science more usable

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.
But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.
Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.
The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.
The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.
When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.
Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.
This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Open Science Challenges

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.
A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?
To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

Demonstrate scientific reuse. Produce concrete examples of researchers and developers building on publicly funded scientific artifacts, including applications that combine resources across institutions or disciplines.
Learn what makes reuse possible. Identify technical barriers, documentation gaps, interoperability challenges, and successful practices that can inform future research infrastructure, funding decisions, and public policy.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

The first challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026
The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.
Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.
Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.
Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.
Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge
The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

How to Join Project ProtoStar

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.
We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.
Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

1nq520l.title: Protecting the storytellers: Women journalists on the frontline of conflict
1nq520l.content:
Protecting the storytellers: Women journalists on the frontline of conflict

“Every woman journalist driven out of a conflict zone is a peace process that loses its witness,” said Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, addressing the United Nations this week.She urged governments to move beyond promises and take concrete action to protect women media workers in the field.

“When the messenger is a woman, it is sexualized, it's dehumanizing, and it is relentless,” said Ms. Ressa, co-founder of the Philippine news organisation Rappler. As part of Women, Peace and Security Week, she was speaking at a high-level event organised by the Permanent Mission of Greece, gender equality agency UN Women, and the UN education and culture agency, UNESCO, which champions journalist protection.‘Fight before it’s too late’Ms. Ressa, who has faced arrest, legal cases and sustained online attacks, reiterated how intimidation can wear down journalists’ credibility and confidence, threaten their safety and ultimately kill their determination to continue reporting. At the height of the attacks against her, she received 90 hate messages an hour. The attacks illustrate how gender-based abuse can be used to discredit women who challenge those in power.“Kill the messenger to kill the message,” she explained to the event – Every Voice for Peace Counts: New Perspectives on the Women, Peace and Security Agenda.AI enablerArtificial intelligence is adding to the threat, enabling deepfakes, fabricated sexual images, cloned voices and coordinated attacks to spread at scale. According to UN Women data, nearly one in four women human rights defenders, activists and journalists reported experiencing AI-enabled abuse which in time can manifest as physical violence. Recent research highlights how online attacks - once dismissed as “virtual” problems - are now spilling offline, affecting women’s safety, well-being, and ability to participate freely in public debate. Ms. Ressa called for online violence to be treated as such, arguing for stronger accountability for perpetrators and technology companies that amplify abuse, sustained funding for women-led journalism, and the inclusion of women journalists in peace and security discussions.‘This is the moment’Invoking the words of Mzia Amaglobeli, a Georgian journalist who remains imprisoned, Ms. Ressa described how she had held up a copy of How to Stand Up to a Dictator in court when she was unable to speak freely.“What she said from her cell is, fight before it's too late,” Ms. Ressa said. “We're getting there. This is it. This is the moment.”

© UNICEF/Aleksey Filippov
Women report being the victims of online violence.

She called on journalists, civil society, governments and international institutions to stand together against a system that allows attacks on women journalists to go unchecked.“We refuse to be the victim,” she said. “The women here turned the attack into the story, and every time one of us stood up, others stood with us. Courage is contagious. But courage isn't a protection strategy - the nations of the UN are”.The meeting took place 26 years since the adoption of Security Council resolution 1325, which affirmed the importance of women's full participation in conflict prevention, resolution and peacebuilding.Keeping Afghan women's voices aliveFor Afghan journalist and media entrepreneur Hamida Aman, protecting women journalists means ensuring that millions of women are not shut out of public life altogether.When she launched Radio Begum in March 2021, her aim was to create a space where Afghan women could share their experiences and access information relevant to their lives. Since the Taliban takeover, restrictions have made that work increasingly difficult.Citing figures from the International Federation of Journalists, Ms. Aman said the number of women journalists in Afghanistan had fallen from about 2,800 before the takeover to fewer than 700. “Being allowed to operate doesn't mean being free to operate,” she said, describing the scrutiny and administrative obstacles facing Radio Begum. The organisation has been threatened and temporarily shut down, and some colleagues have been jailed for more than six months.“If these journalists disappear, who will speak about the lives of Afghan women? Who will make their voices heard?” Ms. Aman asked.

© Sandra Caligaro 
Once they arrive at the studio, Radio Begum journalists hold their editorial meeting, prepare their shows and go live on air.

Silencing collective storiesProtecting women journalists is not only about individual safety. It is also about whose experiences of conflict are documented, whose voices shape public understanding and whose contributions to peace are recognised.“When women journalists are silenced, the women whose stories they are telling are also silenced,” said UN Women Deputy Executive Director for Normative Support, UN System Coordination, and Programme Results, Nyaradzai Gumbonzvanda. “So, it's not just the silencing of the journalists, it's the silencing of our collective story.”Women in conflict settings are often portrayed as victims, she noted, despite their roles in preventing violence, mediating disputes, sustaining communities and rebuilding societies. When their experiences go unreported, the public sees only part of the reality of war, “half of the picture of peace”. The scale of the problem is stark. According to a recent study by UN Women and UNESCO, 75 per cent of women journalists surveyed had experienced online violence. Forty-two per cent linked online attacks to abuse or assault in the physical world, up from 20 per cent in 2020.

© UNICEF/Diego Ibarra Sánchez
A Ukrainian teenager stands in the rubble of her destroyed school in Zhytomyr.

Meanwhile, between 2013 and 2023, coverage of conflicts grew more than sixfold, yet only 5 per cent of published articles focused on women's experiences of war. Just 0.04 per cent mentioned women leaders in peace processes, according to figures presented at the event. “We are not invisible”, Ms. Ressa told the room of women in New York.Begoñã Lasagabaster, Director of UNESCO's Division for Gender Equality, recalled the exhibition They Told the World About It, documenting almost 200 women journalists from more than 25 countries who reported on the Spanish Civil War 90 years ago. “While much of the world counted battles, these women counted lives – they wrote about hunger, displacement, about what war does to a mother, a father, a child, a city, a country,” she said, and with that “they changed the way the world saw war”. Protection must become actionInternational frameworks for protecting journalists already exist. Yet women journalists continue to face physical violence, legal harassment, psychological trauma and online campaigns designed to discredit their reporting.As the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists approaches on 2 November, UNESCO is preparing to launch a new campaign – Threats Evolve, Impunity Endures – alongside new findings on journalist safety and impunity.“Every voice for peace counts,” said Ms. Ressa, “but a voice only counts if it is heard, if that woman survives being heard.”Watch the event on UN WebTV:

12gemmo.title: Epic Games CEO calls Steam's AI disclosure policies "a political act"
12gemmo.content:
"Forcing developers to write a political statement to be used against them by the hate mob they're helping organize is abhorrent"

Image credit: Epic Games

CEO of Epic Games, Tim Sweeney, has once again slammed Steam's AI disclosure policy, calling the company's position on AI disclosure "a political act".
Responding to a tweet in which someone called Valve's AI disclosure policy "absurd", Sweeney agreed, writing, "forcing developers to write a political statement to be used against them by the hate mob they're helping organize is abhorrent."
In a separate tweet, he added: "The primary use of both categories of disclosures is to drive cancel campaigns against games and deprive them of revenue and livelihood unless they get onboard with the movement's political goals. Yes, blocking free choice to adopt productive technology is a political act.
"Say there is a large contingent of gamers that don't like democrats or, equivalently, republicans. Should Valve force developers to list their political affiliation? Is that pro-consumer?" he added (thanks, IGN)."Do you think that policy would have a positive effect on gaming?"In a separate tweet, Sweeney wrote: "These AI statements are just as partisan as mandatory political essays or forcing developers to list their voting history to drive cancel campaigns and public struggle sessions." Elsewhere, he said that "Epic has been extremely open with all developers and the general public about how we’re using AI".
Sweeney has been outspoken about the use of AI in the games industry, previously arguing that platforms should stop tagging games that make use of AI and that the use of AI in development should have no bearing on how a game is received.
This is not the first time Sweeney has criticized Valve's policies, either. Back in June, he suggested Valve's decision to have disclosure labels for projects on Steam that make use of AI was "really irresponsible".
"I think it's really irresponsible of Valve," he said at the time. "They shouldn't do it, because it makes it much, much, much harder for a game developer to have a chance of success. You have to choose from either not using tools that can make you way more productive, and probably failing due to competition that does."

vk9jt9.title: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition was "not a Creative Assembly developed game," says Total War VP after it was pulled amid generative AI concerns
vk9jt9.content:
"We took our eyes off its external development, with all our teams focused on our next big projects," says Roger Collum

Image credit: Sega/Creative Assembly

Creative Assembly has issued a statement regarding the use of generative AI in Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition, which led to the game's removal from sale last week.
Total War vice president Roger Collum clarified that Shogun 2 – Complete Edition "was not a Creative Assembly developed game," and that it "wasn't subject to our same internal reviews and quality assurance."
"We took our eyes off its external development, with all our teams focused on our next big projects," he wrote on the Total War subreddit. "However, whatever the development arrangements, Total War is our franchise and our name is on it."
"We've pulled a small team of senior developers together to work with Sega and the external developer on the next steps."
As noted by Rock Paper Shotgun, Collum does not name the external developer involved with Shogun 2 – Complete Edition. However, Warsaw-based Mataboo Games is listed as a co-developer on the game's Steam page.
Mataboo Games provides "complete end-to-end development support," including design, content creation, gameplay, programming, bug fixing, implementation, porting, and optimisation.
The studio has contributed to several games, including The Blood of the Dawnwalker, Gotham Knights, Suicide Squad, Blair Witch, Stalker: Legends of the Zone trilogy, and Tchia.
In his post, Collum clarified Creative Assembly's stance on generative AI. "We are a craft studio. Our games are made by incredibly talented people, and we do not believe in a world where technology replaces the creativity of humans."
"We do not use generative AI to create game assets, including AI-generated art. We demand the same f any external developers we work with. The situation with Shogun 2 – CE is being investigated."
Collum added: "We use AI tools where they help our craftspeople do their best work, as part of a continual evolution of how we use tools and technology in an evolving and competitive space. For me, the principle is pretty simple: AI can support the creator. It shouldn't replace the creator. I don't believe that AI can replace the human experience, judgement, and creativity that awesome experiences come from. Can AI tools help with analysis, debugging, or speedy prototyping so our experts can focus on making incredible games? Absolutely."
Collum concluded by asking players not to direct their anger or frustration toward individual developers at Creative Assembly.
"When the team does well, it's all about them. When we get it wrong, it's on me. You absolutely have the right to be mad, and to criticise us, but direct it at me. We know we must earn your trust by making good games, and crucially, by how we respond when we get things wrong. We're human, and we will get things wrong, and I promise as long as I'm here, when that happens, we'll hold our hands up and try to make it right."
As previously reported, Shogun 2 – Complete Edition was removed from sale last week amid concerns about the use of generative AI and other performance issues.
Sega and Creative Assembly issued a joint statement, saying the game had "fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards."
"We are working closely with our development partner to identify the cause of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 – Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War."

2ho8x5.title: Report explores how Roblox can maintain older players as it becomes most-played game by total hours in H1 2026
2ho8x5.content:
80% of Roblox's older audience spent money on games in the past six months compared to 59% of non-Roblox players according to Newzoo and GEEIQ data

Image credit: Sega/Gameloft/Roblox

Roblox generated 4.05 billion hours of playtime across PC and console in H1 2026, making it the most-played game by total hours.
Data from Newzoo and GEEIQ shows that Roblox has attracted a valuable cohort of players over 16, with 80% spending money on games in the past six months compared to 59% of non-Roblox players.
A joint report from both firms examines Roblox's maturing audience, how it can maintain it, and the implications for traditional game publishers.
Newzoo market analyst Tianyi Gu said the combined data shows that Roblox's maturing audience "differs from traditional PC and console audiences" and is "particularly driven by entertainment IP."
GEEIQ reports that Roblox averages 14 million concurrent users across 6.7 million active experiences, with 7 million in the top 50 experiences.
When looking at visits since January 1, 2026, these experiences are "dominated by long-running live-service titles rather than new launches."
The report found that most lapsed Roblox players move to other live-service titles like Fortnite and Minecraft, while 30% prefer realistic shooters such as Call of Duty and Grand Theft Auto Online, which "signals a latent demand for AAA-style action."To retain its maturing audience, Roblox is investing in improved graphics and age verification. Roblox Reality, an AI-driven upscaler, is expected to convert titles to photorealistic graphics, with an early version planned for release later this year or in early 2027.
Regarding age verification, Roblox's Q2 results reflected the short-term costs of implementation, including lower-than-expected average bookings per daily active user under 13, as the company prioritises long-term retention over short-term monetisation.

Roblox generated 4.05 billion hours of playtime across PC and console in H1 2026 | Image credit: Newzoo

GEEIQ also analyzed 553 media and entertainment activations on Roblox and found only 15 video game industry activations from 10 brands since 2021.
Of those 15, Ubisoft accounted for five, four of which were integrated into existing Roblox experiences.
In contrast, Gamefam developed and published Sonic Speed Simulator using Roblox Studio. Since its 2022 release, it has become Roblox's largest branded launch and the first branded game to surpass one billion visits in 2024.
Overall, the report surmised that "Ubisoft relied on fast, repeated integrations and Sega on a four-year owned-world commitment; the other eight built a world once and largely stopped there."
"Taken together, none of this means Roblox is coming for AAA's audience next quarter," the report said. "The overlap data is clear that it isn't, yet."
"But the audience is real, it is ageing, and the brands testing it now are running the closest thing to a live experiment on what this generation responds to. That is worth watching closely, even for those with no plans to build on Roblox themselves."

noeks7.title: Is AI really reshaping the developer market?
noeks7.content: The developer job market in 2026 is smaller than it was four years ago. It is also harder to hire the engineers you need. Even though US software development job postings sit about 24% below their pre-pandemic level (which means the competition for tech talent among companies is lower), 87.5% of the tech leaders Lemon.io surveyed call hiring engineers “difficult” or “very difficult”.Do these facts have the same AI cause? Yes, partially.In 2024–2025, AI took over much of the routine coding that juniors and mid-level devs used to do. At theme time, the bar for everyone else was raised. As a result, companies now prefer to have fewer seniors who are fluent in AI tools and keen on their specific business context—rather than an army of cheaper “rising stars”.The market for technical talent has experienced several radical turning points in recent years.First, the pandemic pushed businesses to digitalize fast, so demand for developers rose sharply between 2020 and 2022. At the time, the standard way to deliver tech solutions was to rely on an internal full-time team. And the common strategy was to hire junior and mid-level developers and promote the best among them to senior roles—they’re already familiar with your business niche.Speed was the priority, so many companies hired dozens of devs at once to form teams and accelerate digital transformation. Others were hiring several juniors to help existing teams deliver faster.The peak came in February 2022, when US software development job postings reached roughly 134% above the pre-pandemic baseline, according to Indeed Hiring Lab.The picture is different now. The developers in highest demand are senior and lead-level specialists who can use AI as a force multiplier or to automate routine processes in their workflows.Software Engineering Demand Dynamics by Seniority Level (2022 vs. 2025/2026)Seniority levelDemand change (2022 vs. 2025/2026)Of the total shareReasonJunior, 0–2 yrs exp−64% decline in job postings ⬇️Dropped from 15% of all software hires to 7% ⬇️• Automation of entry-level tasks• High cost of senior mentorshipMid-level, 3–5 yrs exp−13% decline in job postings ⬇️Fell modestly from 46% to 40% ⬇️• Role expectations shifted to AI orchestration, system integration, and cloud management—candidates are still keeping upSenior / Lead, 5+ yrs exp+11% growth in demand ⬆️Grew from 37% to 43% ⬆️• High need for system architecture, security, business logic oversight, and review of AI-generated codeSources: Stanford Digital Economy Lab, Harvard/NBER, IndeedThe engineers most often sought today are genuinely senior. These roles require:Sound decision-making.Ownership of development tasks end-to-end.Sensible integration of AI.Assessment of security risks.A deep understanding of the product the company sells, as well as its marketing context.The widespread fear that AI would wipe out developer roles has proven only partially true. For several years, companies experimented with AI. Now that they are moving toward full integration, they need more tech talent to implement changes.However, the developer’s role is currently transforming too. AI-augmented coding has replaced much of the handwritten code. So knowing AI tools is now as important as knowing a programming language or a framework.There’s also a growing need for engineers with expertise in one’s commercial domain—be it fintech, healthcare, or retail—and those who have profound communication skills to work shoulder to shoulder with marketers and analysts in companies’ cross-functional teams.Tech specialists no longer develop in a straight line from junior to senior to lead.The junior and mid-level tiers are growing slowly because companies prefer to hire experienced, expensive specialists who can handle complex tasks immediately rather than juniors, according to the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. Employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in the occupations most exposed to AI is about 19% below trend, while experienced workers show no comparable gap.So where are seniors coming from in the AI era? There are four typical profiles of candidates you might spot today:Developers who grew into seniors at their last job. Former juniors and mid-levels who gained their experience before the ladder narrowed. We wonєt see many engineers of this type in the coming years.Established seniors. There are few of them, and the bar usually starts at three or more years of relevant experience. They were already senior before AI advanced.Graduates of top computer science programs, such as Stanford, MIT, Carnegie Mellon, and UC Berkeley. Those are getting jobs right away and can be considered senior-level experts even though they didn’t spend years in the process.Engineers with domain expertise. This is the newer path—years of domain experience are becoming increasingly important to companies, especially those operating in highly regulated industries.The disrupted talent pipeline is a direct consequence of AI, which lets anyone create software, but successful products are those that most precisely match their target audience’s needs.One of the clearest signals of AI fluency is which specific tools a developer mentions and whether those mentions hold up under questioning. We at Lemon.io, a marketplace for hiring senior pre-vetted software engineers across 100+ tech stacks, tracked more than 1,500 candidate profiles and compared Q1 2025 with Q1 2026.An analysis reveals that developers are rapidly transforming their resumes to highlight AI-native workflows and agentic capabilities over traditional coding skills.The most explosive growth occurred in AI orchestration, where mentions of the multi-agent frameworks LangGraph and LangChain skyrocketed. Candidates are also aggressively adopting AI-first development environments—led by dramatic surges in Cursor (+643%) and Claude Code (+483%).On top of this, to showcase immediate value as AI integrators, developers increasingly list direct API integrations, with Google’s Vertex AI jumping 238% and new additions like the Claude and Gemini APIs making their first appearances on developer CVs in 2026.Finally, operational MLOps skills saw significant gains, highlighted by a triple boost in MLflow as candidates position themselves to manage and track production-ready models at scale.However, CV tool mentions are not the same as knowing how to apply them to deliver measurable business results. With AI becoming the best friend of senior engineers, vetting their engineering mastery became tricky. One of the approaches pre-vetted developer marketplaces are using is evaluating skills during live tech interviews conducted by other tech leads (Lemon.io’s approach).AI has changed the speed at which new products appear. Even a non-tech founder armed with nothing but an idea can now build an MVP in a few days; a senior-level engineer with architectural thinking and AI skills can deliver a functioning, launch-ready product alone and then maintain and gradually improve it—without any additional engineering help.And when it comes to complex products or corporate migration, it’s enough to have a small team that is professional, well-coordinated, creative, and experienced in the field. Carta’s data shows how lean early teams have become: the median seed-stage startup now has four employees. And it is not the only thing that AI has changed.In 2026, companies are more often diversifying their hiring. They bring on board architects and tech leads as permanent staff. Yet getting a new product ready before market surges, optimizing a specific solution, and doing small non-priority fixes are often assigned to contractors.Working with freelancers also solves another problem: the relatively shallow local pool of developers. AI engineers, full-stack developers with a fintech background, or WordPress builders are simpler and easier to find when you cast your net broadly.Another serious change concerns CTOs and tech leads. It used to be assumed that these people disliked freelancing and were almost impossible to find on remote contractor platforms.After the waves of layoffs that rolled through the tech giants, many highly qualified specialists chose to leave corporate employment. They found more stability in picking their own projects as independent contractors. As a result, hiring dedicated senior talent or leads from global marketplaces is a good idea for companies struggling to find the required talent nearshore.Major tech layoffs by US market giants, 2022–2026CompanyLayoff wavesJobs cutAmazon457,000Intel331,000Meta330,000Microsoft425,000Alphabet (Google)rolling15,000Source: TrueUpNot every role is equally hard to close. The bottleneck lies in highly specialized roles, particularly in AI and cybersecurity, and it directly affects revenue.According to our latest research, based on over 23,000 live job posts by 116 tech companies in September 2026, it takes the longest to find AI engineers. In particular, an AI engineer position sits vacant for a median of 74 days, the longest among all tracked titles in 2026.Product security engineers follow at 62 days—demand for this role has skyrocketed recently due to AI-related risks.The hardest-to-fill tech roles in 2026RoleDays the vacancy stays open (median across companies)Gap between faster and slower companies (days)AI Engineer7428Product Security Engineer6251Machine Learning Engineer5045Engineering Manager5039Technical Program Manager4843Software Engineer4436Source: Lemon.ioThe time gap between faster and slower companies matters as much as the first. Companies differ widely in how efficiently they source talent. Slower-hiring firms lag up to 51 days behind faster competitors when hiring product security engineers and 45 days behind when hiring machine learning engineers.The gap is narrowest for AI engineers, at 28 days. That suggests the delay is due to a market-wide shortage and not a process problem: even efficient companies wait a long time.The financial consequences reach beyond technical roles into leadership. An engineering manager position that stays open for 50 days or more leaves over $23,000 in undelivered business value on the table.AI did not remove the core need for developers, but it changed which developers are needed. The market now rewards a small number of senior engineers who direct AI tools, own technical decisions, and understand the business—and there are not enough of them on the job market, especially if you hire locally and full-time.For companies planning their next hires, there are several practical conclusions:Hire for judgment, not for a list of tools. Mentions of AI tools in CVs are growing by hundreds of percent per year. Yet, the mention itself doesn’t guarantee AI competence. Ask what a candidate shipped and what it changed for the product. Another option: ask them to resolve a tech task in real time with AI tools.Keep the core team small and senior; hire dedicated developers for well-scoped tasks. Put architects and tech leads on staff and bring in contractors for acceleration, non-critical fixes, and optimization.Look beyond the local market. Remote hiring reaches senior specialists, including fractional CTOs, whom you would otherwise have to win over from large corporations.Fix your own process. For most roles, the gap between fast and slow companies is 36 to 51 days. Much of the delay is self-inflicted.One caution belongs here too. Companies that stop developing junior and mid-level engineers entirely are drawing down a pool of seniors that no one is replenishing. Whoever keeps a path open for growing talent will have an advantage when today’s seniors become even scarcer.

2ppjsp.title: Vivrato: 97% of studio leaders use AI in some form during development in EU and North America
2ppjsp.content:
New data finds 94% of have utilised AI across the nine production stages of game production

Image credit: Fotis Fotopoulos via Unsplash

97% of studio leaders have used AI in some form during development, with 94% having used AI in at least one of the nine production stages.
This data comes from a new AI adoption report by consultancy firm Vivrato, based on 101 interviews with studio leaders in Europe and North America conducted between April and September 2026.
The interviews addressed six types of AI: generative AI, rules-based automation, fine-tuned or custom-trained models, classical machine learning, retrieval-augmented systems, and agentic systems.
Vivrato clarified that a "studio's view of generative AI isn't treated as its view of AI overall."
Among the nine production stages, AI is most commonly used in code and engineering (engine, tools, gameplay code) at 86%, followed by general productivity tasks (such as documentation, email, meetings, and planning) at 83%, and concept and pre-production (ideation and brainstorming) at 79%.
Design and prototyping (mechanics, systems, features) use is 68%, while art, assets, and animation (characters, environments, motion capture) are at 60%.
More than half of studios use AI for QA and testing, as well as for narrative and world building. Analytics and player data, along with LiveOps and monetisation, have the lowest AI adoption rates.
Over half of respondents rate the integration of AI into the full production pipeline at three or lower out of ten.

European studios report deeper AI adoption than North America | Image credit: Vivrato

European studios report deeper AI adoption, with an average self-rated pipeline integration depth of 4.2 out of 10 (including the UK), compared to 3.5 out of 10 in North America.
European studios use AI more than their North American counterparts in code and engineering, design and prototyping, art, assets and animation, and analytics and player data.
"The interesting question isn't around which game studios are using AI anymore," said Vivrato founder and CEO Adam Boyes. "Most of the leaders we spoke with declared that they have adopted some form of AI within their development pipelines."
"The focus is now where they're using it, what is changing, what's actually helping, and where teams are still running into challenges."
Boyes added: "We've noticed this year, public discourse and definitions about AI in games usually defaults to generative AI: chatbots, image generation, and synthetic voices."
"However, we know that studios use AI in a variety of ways, from machine learning that predicts player churn to rules-based automation in testing, with very different results – that makes now the right moment to set a clear baseline."
Earlier this week, Sheridans partner Anna Poulter-Jones provided an overview of the current laws surrounding AI in game development.
