166phiw.title: Don't forget about the UI for AI
166phiw.content: ChatGPT Space is a newly launched collaborative workspace within ChatGPT and Codex that allows software engineering teams and their active AI agents to work together in real-time.Connect with Andrew on X.Ryan Donovan: If solving difficult problems is what drives you, Raytheon is hiring software, systems, and hardware engineers to take on some of today's most complex technical challenges. Explore opportunities at careers.rtx.com/raytheon.Ryan: Hello and welcome to the Stack Overflow podcast, a place to talk all things software and technology. I'm your host Ryan Donovan, and I'm here at the OpenAI Dev Day 2026. We're going to be talking about the new unified ChatGPT work app, and also something new they announced today. So, my guest for that is Andrew Ambrosino. He's a member of the technical staff here at OpenAI. So, welcome to the show.Andrew Ambrosino: Thanks for having me.Ryan: Of course. So, before we get into it, can we do a little flyover of how you got into software and technology?Andrew: I mean, I grew up with all sorts of this stuff as a kid.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: Did a lot of early website developments when I was in high school. Got a degree for computer science, did a lot of design, and now I'm here. And I work on the desktop app, I work on Space, work on Codex, all great things.Ryan: Yeah, I think there was a... I don't know if outcry is the right word, when the ChatGPT app and the Cowork app merged together.Andrew: Mhm.Ryan: I think Codex merged with that too, is that right?Andrew: Yeah.Ryan: What was the sort of reasoning behind that?Andrew: Where we want to go is to build one place that you can come, and type in what you need...Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: ...Or speak what you need, and have our most powerful models and artists put that together for you. And that's across software development, that's knowledge work, that's quick questions and answers.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And you shouldn't have to worry about how much reasoning, or which mode you're in in all of this. And so, that's kind of what has been in our heads as we've tried to take ChatGPT as it has existed for years...Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: ...With over a billion consumers, and then this Codex app that was really taking off at the start half of this year.Ryan: Right. And then the Codex for work app, which was sort of Codex...Andrew: Yeah.Ryan: Was there something different with it?Andrew: ChatGPT Work was us bringing all of the power of the Codex harness to a broader audience. Both through the brand, ChatGPT, that people were very familiar with, but also through taming some of the raw nature of the coding agents.Ryan: Yeah, yeah.Andrew: And like, you know, things that just kind of get in the way of it feeling nice to use day to day for a lot of people. So, that's been ChatGPT Work. It's been wildly loved. There was a bit of a, you know, a lot of thoughts about how we might merge the apps, and we're certainly not done there.Ryan: Sure. Yeah. Because it's still two tabs right now.Andrew: Yes.Ryan: Something interesting I noticed, I was using it the other day, and it was like, ChatGPT did this huge complex thing, it's like, you want the other tab. I was like, that's interesting, to have it have that logic built in.Andrew: Yeah.Ryan: I don't know if it's the logic or if it's the model.Andrew: The in variants for us are that, type in chatgpt.com and you type in something that needs a quick answer, you need to get it right away.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And on the other side of the house, if you want to build this giant thing and you need the best of Astra and the best of Codex, you need to be able to do that.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And the minute we feel like it's the right time to make this continuous spectrum that can do both of those without a toggle, we are going to do that. In the meantime, we're not going to shove these things together before we can deliver on that promise, right? We're not going to say, hey, everybody's got this, like, long thinking, reasoning trail of Codex, when they're trying to get a search result.Ryan: Yeah. The press conference, there was sort of a hint at future model routing being built in. Do you do any of that now?Andrew: You know, we have a history with the routers in ChatGPT. We've tried certain things multiple times. But we've got a lot of really cool things coming here. I think that's what I find myself wanting, is not to touch these things.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: Wanting to see code when it makes sense and not when it doesn't, right?Ryan: Everything operates in the browser, right? So why a desktop app?Andrew: Yeah, this has been an interesting one because people just don't download that many desktop apps anymore, right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: Ours has been a wild success. I think the big part has just been some of the breakthroughs on computer use. Some of the advantages that, locally running agents, especially the first half of this year, writing code on your computer with your files and your git checkout, and clicking around in your browser to test the results, right? This is something that is a lot easier to do with the desktop service that we have, and we kind of break out of the box that the browser gives us.Ryan: You know, just because of the security system on my laptop, that Codex specifically uses a lot of Node.js calls.Andrew: Mhm.Ryan: That wouldn't really be possible in a browser, would it?Andrew: We've had this multi-layered system where we've got the Codex harness, which is open source, running on your computer. We're able to do things like this, right? That we wouldn't be able to do in the browser. And then, you know, today we're taking that, we're bringing a cloud version of Codex back into the fold. So that, you on the browser now can use Codex in the cloud environments. Codex Cloud can use your computer if you're like, hey, I've got this checkout on my computer, I don't want to wait for you to set up environment.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: It'll just use your computer, which is pretty neat.Ryan: When you say use your computer, use your computer outside of the browser? Or within the browser?Andrew: If you've got the desktop app open, it can serve as kind of a bridge to your computer and your browser.Ryan: Yeah, I was going to say, you're breaking out that V8 sandbox there, right? (Laughs)Andrew: (Laughs) Sandbox is very important.Ryan: Yeah. Is there any sort of thought for inbuilt sandboxing on the desktop app?Andrew: We were the first to have, like, a relatively functional windows sandbox. That was a pretty hard one.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And we've been working with a few parties on that. We've got a few things in the works.Ryan: Yeah. I mean, I know there's a lot of talk about it, a lot of companies that will sell you a sandbox.Andrew: Mhm.Ryan: So, for the new thing announced today that you're part of, the spaces, what's the change from the desktop app?Andrew: We've found ourselves bouncing between a lot of different tools all day long, right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: Sending stuff on Slack, or jumping into these other tools.Ryan: The way it's always been. Right.Andrew: Yeah. And connecting over MCP, and hoping that the MCP is good, to certain software, right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And we wanted to build a fully collaborative workspace within ChatGPT and Codex. And so we've launched ChatGPT Space, which allows you to make a spot for you and your team to collaborate in real time, both with the other people in your team, and also everybody's agents that are running and everybody's dots that they now have. There's some really cool aspects to this that I'm happy to dive in about, but we really found ourselves wanting to close this loop a little tighter as we were working together all day long.Ryan: You know, everybody is talking about multiplayer AI right now.Andrew: Mhm.Ryan: It's a big one. But, I think when they talk about it, they sort of envision, like, a group chat or a shared terminal or something.Andrew: Yep.Ryan: This is a little different, right?Andrew: It's a little bit different. With space, we're focused a lot on, you know, you've got your agent chat that has your own memory, that's built in, and your own tools and your own preferences, and you might be using that to collaborate with other people on artifacts, like pages, or like sites, or other types of docs that we're bringing to this, like slides.Ryan: Right.Andrew: And this allows you to collaborate on planning. For, if you're doing a big feature and you want to align the team up front, we've got this really great live pages format. What we're not doing right now is bringing people into the literal same chat that you have, and having to fight over who's talking to the agent.Ryan: Right.Andrew: Whose connectors are you using, and whose memory are you using? And, you know, a lot of times what happens with those is, you end up with the lowest common denominator on the connections, right? And so we're saying, hey, you're going to work with your agent on collaborative stuff with the rest of the team. And your dot to work on these artifacts.Ryan: What was the sort of technical complexity you ran into with like, inviting everybody else to collaborate with a single agent?Andrew: Yeah. I mean, we built a full-on, like, CRDT system in five, six weeks? Which is... Probably would have been unheard of months ago.Ryan: CRDT is what?Andrew: Yeah, it's basically, you know, you've got these real-time systems where you're collaborating on docs character by character, and you need live cursors, and you need it to be able to handle, like, little blips, and offline status and things of that nature. We built that out. I think a lot of the stuff that we spent time on, too, was, how does this feel with the agent in the loop? Right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And can I tag in my dot by name? And say, hey, you know, I'm writing this document now, and right here, I want you to drop a graph of our weekly users. And have the dot go off, do the research in your systems, come up with a live chart that's interactive. And drop it on the page, and show you, kind of, where it got edited, and then iterate and say, hey, I don't like this exactly the way it is, can you redo it?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And then have someone else come in, and... Like a lot of this was really about the interaction design, too. You know, it's a little bit product design, it's a little bit technical. It's like, how do you make this feel right?Ryan: The technical details of that sort of real-time interaction, I think, can get complicated. Like, somebody who is our chief product officer used to work at AOL. And when they introduced the three dots that they're typing...Andrew: Mhm.Ryan: ...It crashed the servers.Andrew: Yeah.Ryan: Because every time you did a key press, it sent a message, it pinged everybody else, pinged the servers. So I wonder how you thought about and implemented that sort of like, constant interaction.Andrew: We've got a great infra team that's scaled out ChatGPT to over a billion users daily. We're getting pretty good at this. I think that, you know, there were a lot of hiccups along the way. These things aren't something that you build by yourself in an afternoon, right?Ryan: Yeah. Yeah.Andrew: Even with the most capable models. I think, though, a product like this really was only something that unlocked with Astra. Every model that comes along for us unlocks a certain size of project and speed of project, and this was one of them, that Astra was really kind of the first time that we felt like we could move fast enough on something like this to deliver a great experience.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: There was also, like, the question of, if you've got multiple agents that are also collaborating with you on a doc, that multiplies the load.Ryan: Sure.Andrew: Potentially. Because even something that would have been a single-player doc, that you could have much of the pipeline being local on the edits, all of a sudden you've got this cloud agent that's also collaborating with you on the dock, right? So you're dealing with kind of a multi-agent world. Yeah.Ryan: You know, it's the agents, which one responds to what?Andrew: Exactly.Ryan: And then the updating. It's like, does everybody have the same view at every time?Andrew: Right.Ryan: Was that ever an issue?Andrew: It's funny, like, a lot of the stuff here that we built reminded me of the computer use stuff that we introduced to Codex maybe six months ago. The cursor being a great example. So, one thing that people have really loved about Codex computer use is it's got this really fluid, smooth cursor that...Ryan: Yeah. Yeah.Andrew: ...You know, runs around the screen. And if you think about it, that cursor is largely unnecessary.Ryan: Yes.Andrew: The model does not need that. Like, we are making up a cursor.Ryan: Sure.Andrew: And in some cases, it might even add a little bit of latency, right? Because, you know, you're smoothing out the animation as the cursor comes to a button. Adds a few milliseconds here and there, but it's... Something about it, it makes you able to feel it, and it internalizes, like, what's going on here? And so, the same thing happens here, which is that the model... You know, you give it tools to edit these pages. And one might be, let's say, find and replace, right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And so it's like, alright, can find and replace stuff over a whole doc.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: But you really do want to add a slight, like, you know, animation, so you can say, oh, these five things just changed and you can kind of feel it, right? You add that on top. It's like a bridge from here to there.Ryan: I've heard that described in a game design article years, maybe over a decade ago, being juicy. You know, solid interaction design.Andrew: Right. Yeah. And it's stuff that's, you know, not obvious until you're having an agent edit a doc alongside of you. And it's, you know, text is changing, and you don't see what's changing, and things are jumping a little bit, and it's like, it's not right.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: You have to play with it for a long time.Ryan: So besides having the, like... The little things that make it just kind of feel better, what were the major concerns with, like, the interaction on this multiplayer space?Andrew: That was a big one, obviously. How cursors behave in a document like this. There's just a lot that goes into this stuff. And, for example, if you are tagging your agents in a bunch of spots in the doc, you want copies of it to work in parallel. You know, you don't have to wait for this change before this change, before this change.Ryan: Right. Right.Andrew: But then, how do you get back to these things, right? The agent needs you to reply to it. Are these all separate threads, or are they the same thing? Right? So we've played a lot there, and we'll probably iterate even more as we go. We've played with this a little bit with the dots, and we've got these amazing renders now, of your personal assistant, right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And it's, you know, we tried attaching those to the cursors, and it's a little bit busy, but... I think, you know, we're going to play with this a lot. This is not the final version of the product. Like, we're going to be doing a lot here. I come from the startup world. Like, this is the only way I know how to build, is just to put something out there. And I think we have a damn good V0 here. But I just, I can't imagine, like, not coming back week over... I mean, this is how we were when we launched the Codex app back in February. We did Codex Thursdays for a long time.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: Where it was just, every single week we were just like, we've added this, we've fixed this. Like, tell us what you want. And we just kept going. And I think that's a big reason why it took off.Ryan: Yeah. It's a nice looking desktop app, right? Like, it's almost like the iPod moment, right? You have something that is easier to use, good to look at. How much did that factor into, like, the thing you were making?Andrew: A lot. And we were simultaneously designing ChatGPT Space, same time as dots. At the same time that we're rolling out this new sidebar. At the same time that we were completely rewriting ChatGPT for the browser as well.Ryan: Sure.Andrew: So we're doing all of these things at the same time. And so there was a lot of iteration on, like... This version of sidebar is not going to work for these two products that are coming out, that are also themselves being iterated on in real time. So, I mean, I think we had over 20 launches today, and all these things are happening at the exact same time.Ryan: Right.Andrew: There's no grand design for when they're going to be on desktop. They kind of come together, and the spiral gets a little tighter as we get closer. But my team that works on the desktop app has been involved in all these launches. And this app that we try to make feel very simple has so much in it.Ryan: The speed of development is definitely a big change. Like, we were here talking about Stack Internal and how we built it with Codex.Andrew: Yeah.Ryan: And built it super fast. But I wonder, like you said, you're doing Codex services, all these things you're putting in it, is it too fast for folks like me to catch up with?Andrew: You know, our goal is always to make things that feel easy to use, that feel agent native. So, you know, even if you don't know that we put out this multiplayer pages document type, right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: If it's easy for your agent to use, next time you ask for something to be written, it uses it and you're like, wow, this is great. I didn't even know about it, but it's built in, it's smooth, and now I do, right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: To your point, like, I do think we've entered an era where software can be built so quickly that it's going to be hard. And there will be things that we will have to slow down. Pace, to use the word. But like, just on the software side, too.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: Like, you don't want a new feature every day.Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And, I think shaping these things as they come out is going to be a big challenge. If everyone at your organization has tokens to just make anything that they want, like, consumers and even prosumers can't bear that, right? It's too much.Ryan: It's just overwhelming. Yeah.Andrew: Yeah.Ryan: With your sort of focus on, like, the smoothness of the cursor, and the, like, making it look good, the interaction design, there's a level of judgment and taste that you need to apply to that. And hopefully AI is not going to take that from us.Andrew: Hasn't yet.Ryan: Hasn't yet. (Laughs)Andrew: No, I do think a lot of times this is the bottleneck for us, too. We've got all sorts of explorations, and it's the judgment taste that says, okay, these three can shape together in this way. And like, this one over here, well, it's not quite there yet.Ryan: Right.Andrew: I think that's the big challenge.Ryan: And with the speed and ease of creating things, the taste is both going to be more valuable and harder to apply, I think. How do you think about making something, Spaces or the unified app, desktop app, like, a tasteful, good experience for a user?Andrew: Well, I think the most important thing we do at OpenAI is, we use everything ourselves a lot, right?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: We're a big company now, and we try to be very honest about the product market fit we have internally before we put things out. If it's not there, then it's important for us to not say, oh, well, you know, somebody else will like it, right? Because you can rationalize anything.Ryan: Sure.Andrew: And be like, well, it didn't work in here. But we really try to keep ourselves grounded, and like, is this something that everybody internally is loving?Ryan: Yeah.Andrew: And if not, like, what gets us there?Ryan: Yeah. And I think for some of the developers listening, they don't really care about the prettiness or the comfort of the interface. They're just like, raw terminal folks. You're not pushing them out of their terminal, are

tpjh3d.title: Japan Actors Union announces guidelines addressing unauthorised use of generative AI to replicate voice performances
tpjh3d.content:
"Technological advancements will not stop, but the 'living, breathing human expression' and 'respect for rights' must always remain at its core"

Image credit: Ritupon Baishya via Unsplash

The Japan Actors Union has announced new guidelines to address the unauthorised use of generative AI to replicate voice performances.
As Automaton reports, the union's framework recommends obtaining prior consent at "every stage" of using generative AI, including before training models on an actor's performance.
If generative AI replicates a performance, it must be treated as a new performance, requiring additional royalties or compensation for the actors involved.
For deceased actors, generative AI may replicate their voice only if permission was granted during their lifetime. Developers or AI companies must also obtain consent from the deceased's family and affiliated agency or company, and pay royalties.
The union's guidance also covers automatic translations by generative AI into another language. If used, it must maintain the "artistic integrity" of the original performance and cannot be used overseas without permission.
"The Japan Actors Union will strive to not just establish these guidelines as industry-wide rules, but also strengthen its efforts to encourage the government to legislate regulations that protect 'voice rights'," the union said.
"Technological advancements will not stop, but the 'living, breathing human expression' and 'respect for rights' must always remain at its core."
Last year, research showed that over half of Japanese developers use generative AI in game development, primarily for creating visual assets, images, character art, story generation, in-game text, and programming support.
In 2023, SAG-AFTRA members voted to authorise a strike against several major publishers to protect performers from AI and ensure job security.
After an 11-month strike, members voted in favour of the 2025 SAG-AFTRA Interactive Media Video Game Agreement, which included safety guardrails around AI being put in place, including "consent and disclosure requirements for AI digital replica use and the ability for performers to suspend consent for the generation of new material during a strike."
Yesterday, UKIE announced a partnership with law firm Sheridans to offer an AI Compliance and Accreditation Service, supporting UK studios in using AI lawfully and responsibly.

12itzdb.title: AI says you’re right, formal methods say you’re wrong
12itzdb.content: Quint is an open-source, executable specification language and toolchain based on TLA+ that enables engineers to model, simulate, and verify system behaviors using an intuitive, programmer-friendly syntax.Connect with Gabriela on LinkedIn and X.Congrats to Populist badge winner Alex K. for winning the badge on their answer to SQL Server: Select Top 0?.[intro music]Ryan Donovan: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Stack Overflow podcast, a place to talk all things software and technology. I'm your host, Ryan Donovan, and today we're talking about formal verification for agentic coding using TLA+. My guest for that is Gabriela Moreira, the CEO at Quint. So welcome to the show, Gabriela.Gabriela Moreira: Thank you, Ryan. Thank you for having me.RD: My pleasure. Before we get into the formal verification topic, can you give us a little background? How did you get into software and technology?GM: I started a bachelor in computer science in 2015. I think I had like two ways into software. One of them was because I was customizing my Tumblr themes and I liked changing the code and seeing how things switched in the screen. I thought it was really magical. And then I was like a bit into gaming. My computer was not the best, so I had to like, troubleshoot a lot, and I enjoyed doing that. I was considering either doing mathematics or doing computer science, and I ended up doing computer science, but it was a really hard decision. And I ended up, like, the parts that I like the most about mathematics is the parts that we see about mathematics in computer science, like discrete mathematics, graph theory. So that was nice. And then inside formal, inside software, computer science, I liked like compilers, computer theory. And eventually I was presented with formal methods towards the end of the course and really, really liked TLA+. And then I started working with it like right away. It never stopped.RD: Yeah, I think I ran across TLA+, briefly in researching a sort of jokeyish article about time travel and programming. It's a very, you know, any sort of formal methods proof programming, it seems very strict and sort of intimidating to outsiders. Do you feel that it deserves this sort of intimidating reputation?GM: People make it deserve that often. It's very strong in academia, right? Formal methods of different shapes. And when the academics present that to the industry, they often fail to present it in an accessible way, talk about actual pain points it solves. People talk about like, oh, you have to prove your code correct. What are you doing? You're guilty. So I think the way it's presented is kind of like what makes it deserve that. But in reality, it's actually way more useful for day-to-day people if you know what you're doing. So yeah, I don't think it should deserve that. But I think the current shape of things, it often does.RD: What is TLA+? How does it work?GM: So TLA+ is a formal specification language. Okay, we know probably what a specification is, right? We are specifying what are the requirements of our software, what it should do, what it should not do. But in TLA+, you do that formally. And formally means there is no room for ambiguity. There is no room for interpretation, right? So you're specifying it in a way, and it's that way, and that's it. And the way this is achieved, the lack of ambiguity, is by establishing a formal semantics to the... syntax, right? So whatever you write there, there is one precise way about what this means going all the way back to mathematics and how it's established in mathematics. So really, there's no room for ambiguity. That's how it was born, to be a precise language, to define algorithms, protocols, especially in the distributed systems area. So TLA+ was created by Leslie Lampard, the father of distributed systems, also creator of text for Latex. So Leslie Lampard was writing papers, right? He was coming up with all these distributed systems, algorithms, and he was writing papers and he realized that he was not being precise. He found like imprecision in his own papers. And he's like, oh, if I'm this like super smart person and I'm making this imprecision, so for sure other people are being imprecise as well, and that's a problem. So let's come up with a shared language we can use. So it was just a language used in papers. And then people realized they could add tooling for that. So you can like use machines to check what was written there, not only like be a precise way of writing it, but actually checking properties. So they implemented a model checker, the TLC model checker, which is an acronym that don't stands for anything. They don't define what the acronym stands for, just TLC. That is the model checker for TLA+, which is, you can think of it as like the compiler for a language, right? Languages have compilers. Specification language is they don't have like a compiler that will execute your code or produce executable code. They have something like a model checker, which is going to verify the code, right? So it takes your TLA+ specifications that will define your specification and check that it is correct.RD: If I have it correctly, the formal specification is not something you would build a piece of software off of. You have that first and then have the software later. It would be something to verify that the software you've written meets the specification, right?GM: There is a big problem with formal methods, which is we don't really have something to verify that the actual code is correct. There are some tools for verifying that the actual code is correct, but they are often very limited because the amount of things you can write in code is very big. So it's hard to write, for instance, a model checker for Rust. There exists some model checkers for Rust, but they are often quite limited in how much they can do and how much they can check. In TLA+, you can check much more, like everything you write in the language pretty much. There's some KPIs, but like most things you can write in the language can be checked because it's a language made for that. So it doesn't have such a big scope. You said like you first write your specification and then you go and write your code. And that's like the main pitch for TLA+ mainly, right? So for TLA+, the main pitch is like you go first, you write your TLA+ model, and then later you go and write your code. Leslie Lempore talks about this as who would construct a building before drawing a blueprint. You first need your blueprint, and in your blueprint, you can do some sort of calculations, see if the walls match in size, they add up. You can do all of these calculations, and if you notice something is off, it's much easier to fix a blueprint than to go and fix a building. And that's true also for code, although there are some like, oh, but code is so much cheaper to fix than a building. But like, is it? Because it's very expensive to write code. If you are going to change code, you might introduce bugs. It's very complicated. So you're thinking about a design, you might want to first check the design on a simple abstract level in a formal specification language, and then later you go to implement it. I don't think it's only on this order. I think that's the ideal order. Like you first go and design and then you go and implement. I think this might be one of the reasons why the industry struggles to see the value in formal methods and like, oh, think this is for me because we... people pitch a lot like, oh, you have to do it before. And you're like, oh, but I already have my code. Then what should I do now? But it's still valuable, of course, if you already have your code. You can go and find design issues even after the code is written. And then you go and attempt different fixes, right? So if you found a problem, you can go like, oh, would this be a fix for my problem? You can go and model that in TLA+ or other specification language. And then... oh yeah, no, that's not actually a fix. There's this one case where actually this fix doesn't apply. So I actually have to think about a different fix before you go and apply to the code. So there are different moments in your life and your project lifecycle where you want to use formal specifications.RD:There's some edge cases that don't arise until you sort of hit something like several times. Like it'll only show up in production because of the volume of traffic. So formal specification would be able to catch the faulty logic before it has to go into production, right?GM: So I want to talk about a recent example we had of that, but it's actually, this one was not using TLA+, it was using Quint. So it's a good way maybe for me to introduce Quint. Quint is just a surface syntax on top of TLA+. TLA+ syntax, you can see, is kind of like very mathematical, hard for people to onboard. So it started with a different syntax and also would develop like more tooling on top of TLA+ for like making things easier for industry applications. So it's just another version.RD: TLA+ seems very rooted in like analytic philosophy and logic, right?GM: You want programmers to adopt it and programmers are much more used to writing words and call functions into type mathematical symbols. They think about AND and OR, they don't think about backslash. We started as a syntax and then we added more tooling. It's the same philosophy underneath. We had recently a use case where we have a blog post about this, if you want to read more, but there's basically this bug that was happening with an external team from OpenHands. So OpenHands was having a Kubernetes deployment and it was causing problems. It was like triggering alerts all the time and they had a bug, a race condition. And then they had like some Quince tooling installed and they were to apply a fix. But between applying a fix and then seeing the problem happening again, it would take weeks because of the nature of the deployment. So they decided to check that with Quint if the fix was enough. And Quint said, no, this is not enough. This case is not covered by your fix. It's still going to cause a problem. And actually, they did that after deployment. And then they saw the actual problem that Quint reported happen in production later on. And then they experimented with different fixes until… Quint could verify the fix and then they shipped that fix and they didn't have problems anymore. So this case is where it tells you no, right? We actually posted a meme yesterday that fits well here. We posted a meme that like Claude and ChatGPT and other tools, they will tell you you're absolutely right. But formal method tools, they'll tell you you're absolutely wrong.RD: Right. I think that information is probably better for engineers. Engineers want to know what's wrong with a thing. What's right with it is that's fine. Like, let that go.GM: And it's also helpful if you are trying to make optimizations in your code. So not only applying fixes and checking that fix apply, but applying optimizations and checking that optimizations are not going to break any existing behavior that you have, right? This is a nice case from AWS. So AWS, there's probably like the most famous and strongest user of TLA+. And they wrote this comprehensive paper about the different projects in which they apply TLA+, and what they got out of it. And it's super nice. And like one of the cases that they could apply aggressive optimizations that they wouldn't feel confident in applying if they could not actually check. It's not affecting behavior. It's still holding all properties for all cases. So that was super nice.RD: So AWS is an interesting one because they just hired the creator of the Lean language, which is another formal specification language. Do you have an opinion on the difference between TLA+ and Lean or other formal specification languages like that?GM: I love Lean. I actually learned ROC, like previously COC, when I was also in... my graduation. So I haven't had much contact with Lean, but it's essentially the same thing, just like a little bit better. The same as TLA+, right? So there are different families. So for model checking tools, like TLA+, Quint, Alloy is also one. It's a bit different, but also in there. You can just specify what you want, and then you have automatic proofs. And you don't even have to go all the way to proofs. You can also get value just from like random simulation. So if you're like... you don't have time to go and reduce your state space such that the tool can find a proof for you or like tune the spec until you can actually prove it, you can also get value out of just like running simulations. And this we have a bunch of experience on. We had done a lot of like just simulations and got a lot of value out of specifications. So there is that. And then if you go to the proof assistants like Lean, COC, Isabel, Agda. There you have to put more work in. So besides writing your specification, and also the specification is written usually in a different, like more specific form, and it's harder to write your specification. You also have to go and write your ownproof, which is a lot of work, right? So before, like until last year, it was like, okay, you go to model checking if you want something more lightweight, and then you go to these other tools if you really need to be super thorough with everything. And it was way more reserved to like spaces where safety was super, super important to really not have any flaws. So it was way harder to justify applying that to the industry, right? How can you spend like maybe one year, maybe three years proving something? Does it really justify? Things have changed a lot this year because now you can ask your AI buddies to write the proof for you. And it seems like this is working quite well, right? So it's very interesting. I'm super excited about the… evolutions on like, especially with Lean, a lot of like AI is getting good at writing Lean proofs. There's a lot of debate on things there. But I think like the main point that concerns me with this is who is writing the specifications, right? Because I think in a lot of these scenarios, people are relying on getting AI to also write the specifications and then you get a proof, but it's a proof of what? Did you really check? So I think tools like TLA+ and Quint and Alloy, they can help you iterate a bit more. So especially with Quint, we've done a lot of things just to help you understand what you have specified. So you're not just like spec and then you go and check. You also can understand what's in there. You can like go give me one example run and then you look at that. Does that sound correct? You have like interactive tools. So I think it's way more important now that we understand what is specified and we check like, oh, the specification matches what I intended. And then if I have a proof of that, then perfect. But like, I think the biggest gap now is in this, making sure you're really specifying what you have intended and not like just delegated to AI because people are redoing that a lot. Especially also like with TLA+, there is more adoption than ever now because the syntax was a pain point. Now AI can write it for you. So it kind of like took that pain away. But then if you cannot read what the AI wrote because the symbols are too complicated, then I have a big concern with that.RD: Where do you put the vibe coding, right? The vibe coding here is in the former proof stage. We talked a little bit about this and I think one of the things I've seen in the last year or so is people talking about spec-driven development. You know, with TLA+ being a sort of formal spec, are there ways to use AI to kind of generate code from it? Or I think you're talking about the reverse way of like generating a formal spec from whatever specification you have.GM: Yeah, the two paths are feasible and being explored for the spec-driven development path, right? Where you first write the spec and then produce code out of the spec. It was interesting because like last year, I think around this time or earlier, I think like around April last year, maybe, there was a talk at AI Engineer, like this big AI conference. And the person was proposing like, oh, spec-driven development. This is where the terms arise again. And then I watched the talk and I was very excited. Like, oh, this is a time for specs, finally. And then it was like, oh, no, you write this markdown and you have the agents read the markdown. And I was like, oh, no, markdown. It can be imprecise and then you also cannot really check what was written there. So if more and more people are using agents to write the markdown, are you really going to read the markdown and make sure that matches your intention?RD: The spec in this case is just a larger prompt.GM: Especially if you're not reading it and you're not refining it, it's just like a more agentic output and where does your intention land there. And it's not executable, right? You cannot really, like, I think a lot of joy that comes from programming is, like, you go and write some code, which is your, like, intention. You run it and you get maybe unexpected results. And like, oh, no, that's not what I meant. Let me adjust. The fact, like, when you execute it and you see the results is where, like, you can refine and you're very used to this loop of iteration. And when you remove the execution and you're, like, produce a text document, you have to read a text document, refine it, it's very frustrating. And because it's frustrating, I don't think it's very productive. And I think we will make a lot of mistakes.RD: When I spoke to a creator of C++, he said, English and other human languages are very imprecise. And code is a precise definition of a solution, right?GM: Some people say a precise specification is the code. And I agree with that to some extent. I think there's stuff in the code you don't care so much about. Whether you're calling this function this or that. Now, especially if you're developing a lot with AI, there's stuff in the code you don't care so much about, like whether you're logging things this way or that way as long as they get logged, or there's some small details in code that are not as important as your core algorithm, your core protocol. So when you're just going to code, especially if you're not spending time writing it, if you're iterating with AI, it's very hard to play with the code. It's a lot of code. Get that all in your brain and then see if it's right or not. And it's nice to extract that most important bit, core algorithm, the core protocol, and reason about that in your head while maybe leaving AI to the side some smaller details. And this is also what formal specifications can help you with. They are in a high level of abstraction. So when you see a TLA+, specification is not going to be talking about like, when do you log some line? When you do this, it's not like going to be in all level of detail. It's going to be on the level of the things you actually care about.RD: It's becoming clear, I think, with folks doing a lot of, offloading a lot of the tasks you said, like the specification itself, not just decoding to the AI. A little bit of formal specification understanding is going to become important for everybody. So how do you make formal specification languages like TLA+ a little more accessible for people to understand?GM: Well, there are some layers to it. First thing we tried in our team was to make this different syntax that was more familiar to engineers. And I think that helps if you're going to read the spec. I think it helps a lot, especially if you're writing spec by hand, then for sure it helps a lot. We had like autocomplete, it was easier to write, etc. Now people are probably not going to be writing that by hand. Maybe they'll be reading it. I don't know. The future is kind of unclear. But let's assume they maybe will not

ao72b4.title: MCP standardized tools. Now we need the infrastructure around them.
ao72b4.content: MCP adoption happened extremely fast.Developers can now connect models to repositories, databases, browsers, observability systems, internal APIs, and dozens of other tools through a shared protocol. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code, and a growing list of other clients all speak it. Vendor-hosted endpoints exist for GitHub, Linear, Notion, and many others. The Tier 1 SDKs are approaching half a billion downloads a month.That is a real achievement. For years every AI application built its own tool-calling layer. MCP gave the ecosystem a common interface. Once a server exists, multiple agents can use it without custom glue. That alone is worth the effort.But after building around MCP for coding agents, I started noticing something else. The protocol was becoming standardized faster than the infrastructure around it. Connecting a tool was becoming easy. Running that system reliably across real users, real credentials, and real work was not.The protocol solved a specific problem: how can an AI model talk to tools through a common interface? The next set of problems is different. How do we make thousands of those interactions reliable, secure, efficient, observable, and straightforward to deploy?The happy path looks simple. An agent talks to an MCP client, which talks to an MCP server, which calls a tool that talks to an API or database. In a demo, that is often all you need.In production, the picture changes. You have multiple agents, multiple users, many MCP servers, credentials that must not leak, rate limits, permissions that differ by person or by task, failures, retries, logs, tool schemas that change, context constraints, and machines that are not identical. The mental model becomes something closer to agents and clients sitting in front of authentication, routing or gateways, then a set of MCP servers, then the actual systems those servers touch. Every one of those layers can fail independently.A concrete example: an agent that reads documentation and fails once is annoying. An agent that creates cloud resources, writes database records, or opens pull requests and fails halfway through is a different problem. Partial work, inconsistent state, and the need for idempotency or compensation become real requirements. The protocol does not magically supply them.One pattern I kept seeing is infrastructure duplication. Developers and teams repeatedly build authentication, deployment, connection management, retries, logging, secret handling, health checks, access control, simple registries, caching, and rate limiting. The same pieces appear in different codebases because the protocol standardizes the message format, not the operational concerns around it.This is not unique to MCP. Earlier infrastructure transitions followed a similar shape. Once physical servers became painful enough, cloud abstractions matured. Once every application reinvented authentication, identity platforms matured. MCP may be entering a stage where managing dozens of individual local servers, each with its own configuration and credentials, starts to feel like the old way of doing things. Whether the eventual abstractions live in agent runtimes, cloud platforms, gateways, or somewhere else is still open. The duplication is already visible.Local servers over stdio are easy to understand, close to the user, and naturally connected to local files and processes. They were the perfect way to experiment. Local execution also avoids many of the authentication and multi-tenant problems that appear once the server moves onto the network.Team-scale usage exposes the limits. Everyone needs installation and configuration. Versions drift. Credentials live on different machines. One developer’s server can break differently from another’s. Onboarding becomes repetitive. Observability is fragmented because each machine is its own island. Remote or hosted servers address some of those problems, but they introduce others: authentication that actually works across clients, latency, multi-tenancy, data handling, uptime, permissions, and questions of vendor dependence. Neither model is automatically superior. They solve different sets of constraints.The July 2026 specification changes helped the remote case. Removing protocol-level sessions and the initialize handshake means a remote server can scale more like an ordinary HTTP service. That is useful progress. It does not remove the need for authentication, authorization, or operational discipline.Coding agents need repository context. Naively giving an agent the whole tree creates token cost, irrelevant information, distraction, higher latency, and sometimes worse reasoning. Bigger context windows do not eliminate the problem. The question shifts from “how much can the model hold?” to “which context deserves to be there?”This is where a lot of my early work sat. Hexum.dev began in part around making repository context more efficient, so the agent saw the relevant structure instead of a raw dump of files. On a published 24-task benchmark using MBPP and HumanEval, the measured context sent to the model dropped from 220,393 tokens to 27,352 (an 87.6% reduction) while still passing all official tests. The methodology is public. The number is less important than the observation: once you start treating context selection as a deliberate step rather than a dump, other constraints appear.Developers talk about this constantly now under the banner of context engineering. Progressive or dynamic tool discovery is one response to a related problem: loading every tool schema from every server into the context on every turn. Client best practices now recommend deferring full definitions and providing a search-style meta-tool. The same guidance explains why: progressive discovery can dramatically reduce tool-definition tokens and can improve selection accuracy by keeping the model focused on a smaller set of relevant tools. The pattern is not universal yet, but the pressure is clear.There is a point where giving an agent 50, 100, or several hundred tools becomes harmful rather than helpful. Selection accuracy can drop. Context fills with schemas the model may never need. Name collisions and vague descriptions make the problem worse.Should every tool definition always sit inside the active context? Or should tools themselves be retrieved dynamically? Both approaches exist in the wild today. Static registration is simple when the surface is small. Progressive discovery, semantic search over tool descriptions, and gateway-style routing that exposes a smaller set are all being tried. The protocol itself is moving in this direction through progressive discovery guidance and related work. What remains open is how much of the selection logic lives in the client, in a gateway, in the server, or in the model’s own tool-use training. Least privilege also matters here: an agent that can see every tool is an agent that can be tricked into calling ones it should not have access to.MCP security is not the same as ordinary API security. An agent can read untrusted text, interpret it as instructions, call tools, and mutate external state. That creates surfaces that look like prompt injection, confused-deputy problems, over-broad permissions, malicious or poisoned tool descriptions, secret leakage through arguments or results, and supply-chain risk from the servers themselves.None of this means the protocol is inherently insecure. It means that once natural language can cause software to invoke real capabilities, the trust boundaries and permission model become critical. Least privilege, explicit approval for destructive actions, careful handling of tool results as untrusted input, and authentication that survives the full path from client to server to backend system all matter more than they do for a conventional API. A 2026 measurement study of 7,973 live remote MCP servers found that 40.55% exposed tools without authentication. That is a deployment problem, not a protocol problem, but it is the problem teams actually hit.A human using software notices an error and stops. An autonomous agent may continue. That changes the requirements around retries, idempotency, timeout behavior, partial failure, and validation of tool results. Observability becomes more important because you may need to reconstruct what the model believed, which context it saw, which tools it knew about, which one it selected, what arguments it generated, what the tool returned, and what it did next.Standardized telemetry is starting to appear. OpenTelemetry’s GenAI semantic conventions include MCP-related spans and attributes. Work such as SEP-414 reserves space in _meta for W3C trace context so traces can cross the MCP boundary. The official Python SDK now emits OpenTelemetry spans by default. Whether this becomes the default way teams debug agent-tool systems is still early, but the demand is obvious once agents move past demos.At first I thought one of the main problems was context efficiency. Hexum.dev’s early work on shrinking repository context for coding agents reflected that. Once you optimize context, you run into tool selection. Once you expose tools, you run into deployment and configuration. Once tools are remote, you run into authentication and permissions. Once agents become more autonomous, reliability, security, and observability move to the front. The realization was that MCP is not merely a protocol problem. It is becoming an infrastructure category.Hexum.dev today is a hosted remote MCP endpoint for coding agents. Its scope grew as we ran into adjacent problems around context handling, architecture checks, and controlling agent behavior. The agent still lives in the editor the developer already uses; Hexum.dev sits around specific parts of that workflow. Building it did not eliminate the surrounding problems. It made them concrete.There is one lesson from building Hexum.dev that has nothing to do with protocols.Most of building is uncertainty. Things fail, direction changes, and you spend a lot of time on ideas before anyone validates them. Having friends who listen, encourage you, and challenge you when needed matters more than founders often admit. Yuchen and Pranav have been two of those people for me. They are not building Hexum with me, but they have listened to countless ideas and made the uncertain stretches easier to keep moving through.A possible future stack looks something like this: models and agents at the top, agent runtimes and MCP clients beneath them, then an infrastructure layer that handles routing, authentication, permissions, context management, tool discovery, caching, observability, policy, and reliability, then the MCP servers themselves, then the databases, APIs, code, and SaaS systems those servers touch.This is a hypothesis, not a certainty. Some of those capabilities may end up inside model providers, inside agent runtimes, inside cloud platforms, inside gateways, or inside individual MCP servers. The boundary is not fixed. The interesting part is that the protocol’s success is forcing the question. Once tool interoperability is taken for granted, the remaining work is everything required to make that interoperability production-grade.MCP’s biggest achievement may be that developers are beginning to take tool interoperability for granted. That is what successful standards eventually do. They make a previously hard problem feel ordinary.Standards rarely eliminate infrastructure. They move the infrastructure problem somewhere else. HTTP standardized how systems communicate, but we still built CDNs, load balancers, API gateways, observability platforms, identity systems, and cloud infrastructure around it. MCP may follow a similar path. The protocol gave agents a common language for tools. Now we have to build everything required to make that language reliable at scale.The interface is no longer the hardest part. The systems around it are.
